title: Working as a cigar maker and photo engraver as a boy
summary: Before music he worked at 11 or 12 for his uncle in cigars, disliked the conditions, then at 13 or 14 worked for the Russian photo engraver Romansky making prints for the Sunday paper.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: I saw in -- I think it was what? -- Leonard says that you didn't want to be a musician but your family wanted you to be. Was that -- in Leonard's book? And then I read in Chilton that you worked with a photo engraver before becoming a musician?
I was a cigar maker first.

Yeah. I was a cigar maker. See, I was starting used to work for my uncle first -- in the cigar business, and I started from the ground up. I started to strip tobacco, sift it, sweep the building, and I started to breaking bunches. Then I started to roll them. Then I started making them for myself. And then I went out in the big factory and I was working -- I started on the cheap job which sometimes was $8 a thousand. Then the big job was $50 a thousand. You had to be almost perfect, that when you roll them you could hardly see where you rolled -- how you rolled them. And sometimes you could only make about 15 a day, you know. 25 a day you got to be perfect.

And then the old men, they smoking cigars all through it. They didn't want no ventilation and they spit on the floor and the tobacco's on the floor and all that. And I saw all that and I began to get disgusted and sick of -- and I just quit.

Then I went to work for an old Russian named Romansky. He was a photo engraver and used to work for the newspaper. And I made more money working with him, making prints, you know, for the Sunday paper and all that, and I stayed with him for a couple of years. I was real good.
How old were you when you worked in the cigar factory?
Oh, I was about 11 or 12 years old.
And then when you went to work for Romansky?
